title: The LORD Is My Light and My Salvation
summary: The psalm opens in bold confidence: with the LORD as light, salvation, and stronghold, the psalmist will not fear even if an army surrounds him. His one desire is to dwell in God's house and gaze on his beauty, where God will hide him in the day of trouble. Then the tone shifts to urgent prayer: hear me, do not hide your face, do not forsake me, even if father and mother do. The psalm ends in certainty that he will see God's goodness in the land of the living, and with a call to wait for the LORD.
story: Psalm 27 continues the longing for God's house that runs through Psalms 26 to 28. In Psalm 26 the psalmist loved the place where God's glory dwells; here he asks for only one thing, to live there and gaze on God's beauty. The psalm also gathers up the fear of enemies that has run through Book I since Psalm 3, and it answers that fear not by denying the danger (armies, false witnesses, violence) but by naming who God is. Its closing call to wait for the LORD and be strong and courageous echoes God's words to Joshua as Israel prepared to enter the land (Joshua 1:6-9), applying Israel's great charge to one person's fear.
historical:
The heading reads simply Of David. Traditional readers see David's life behind it: a fugitive surrounded by armies, betrayed by those close to him, and longing for the sanctuary he could not reach. Many modern scholars read of David as a collection heading and leave the date open. The mention of God's tent and temple (verses 4 to 6) points to a setting in Israel's worship, and the false witnesses of verse 12 suggest a legal accusation, like those behind Psalms 17 and 26.

The psalm divides so clearly (confidence in verses 1 to 6, lament in verses 7 to 14) that many scholars think two originally separate psalms were joined. Others argue it was composed as one, pointing to shared vocabulary across both halves (salvation, enemies, heart, seeking, hiding, face) and to the way the second half tests the confidence of the first. Readers on both sides agree that as it now stands, it holds trust and plea together. In Jewish practice Psalm 27 has long been recited during the month of Elul and the High Holy Days in the autumn, as a psalm of repentance and trust.
cultural:
Light was an ancient image for life, safety, and divine favor; darkness for danger and death. The Psalms connect God with light often (Psalm 36:9), but this psalm makes it a personal title: my light. A stronghold was a fortified refuge, and a rock was a high place where enemies could not reach. The tent, tabernacle, and shelter of verse 5 recall the sanctuary as a place of asylum, where a fugitive could take hold of the horns of the altar and be protected (1 Kings 1:50).

Verse 10 speaks to one of the deepest fears in a kinship society. In ancient Israel a person's family was their security, identity, and legal protection. To be forsaken by father and mother was to be utterly exposed. Whether the verse describes an actual abandonment or imagines the worst possible case, its promise is that God receives the one whom even family has left, gathering him in as a kinsman takes in a relative.
literary: The psalm has two halves in contrasting moods. Verses 1 to 6 are a song of trust, spoken about God in the third person, with rhetorical questions (whom shall I fear?) and a single desire at the center (verse 4). Verses 7 to 14 are a lament addressed directly to God in the second person, with urgent imperatives: hear, be merciful, answer, hide not, teach, lead, do not hand me over. The word face links the halves: the psalmist's heart tells him to seek God's face, and he pleads that God not hide it (verses 8 and 9). Verse 13 begins in Hebrew with an incomplete sentence (literally, Unless I had believed that I would see), a word the Masoretic scribes marked with special dots, perhaps because they were uncertain about it. The last verse turns outward and speaks to the reader or to the psalmist's own soul: wait for the LORD.

outline.t: Whom shall I fear? Confidence against armies
One thing I ask: to dwell in God's house
Hear me; hide not your face; do not forsake me
Teach me your way amid false witnesses
I will see the goodness of the LORD; wait for him

doctrines.note: The psalm shows faith as confidence rooted in who God is (light, salvation, stronghold), able to face armies and yet still cry out urgently in fear. Trust and lament are not opposites.
Verse 13 hopes to see God's goodness in the land of the living, in this life, and verse 14 calls for patient waiting. Hope here is patient, active, and courageous.
The psalmist's heart speaks God's own invitation back to him, seek His face, and he answers, Your face, O LORD, I will seek. Prayer is a response to God's invitation.
Verse 10 speaks to the pain of abandonment by parents and promises that the LORD will receive the forsaken. God's care reaches past the failure of every human bond.

words.note: Or, light. In the Old Testament light is associated with God's presence, life, salvation, guidance, and truth. God's first creative word was let there be light (Genesis 1:3), and the priestly blessing asks that the LORD make his face shine on his people (Numbers 6:25). Here the psalmist calls God himself my light.

No'am, beauty, pleasantness, delightfulness. It describes what is lovely and gracious. In verse 4 the psalmist longs to gaze on the beauty of the LORD, not only to be safe with God but to delight in him. The same word appears in Psalm 90:17, praying that God's favor rest upon his people.

Panim, face. In the Bible God's face means his personal presence and favor; to seek his face is to seek him, and for him to hide his face is to withdraw his favor. The priestly blessing prays that God lift up his face on his people (Numbers 6:26). The word ties the psalm's two halves together.

Qavah, to wait for, to hope in with expectation. It appears twice in the final verse, framing the command to be strong and courageous. Waiting in the Psalms is not passive; it is holding on to God while he has not yet acted.

christ: The New Testament does not quote Psalm 27, but its central images are ones Jesus claimed. He said, I am the light of the world (John 8:12), and John describes him as the light that the darkness has not overcome (John 1:5). The psalm longs to dwell in God's house and gaze on his beauty; John says the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory (John 1:14), so that God's presence was seen in a person. The hope of verse 13, to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living, takes on new depth in light of Jesus' resurrection, which brings God's goodness into this world and not only beyond it. The link is thematic rather than predictive, but the psalm's deepest longing, to see God's face, is what the New Testament says is given in Christ, in whose face the glory of God shines (2 Corinthians 4:6).
questions: The psalmist asks for only one thing. If you could ask God for one thing, what would it be, and what does that reveal about your heart?
Verse 10 imagines being forsaken by father and mother. How does the promise that the LORD will receive you speak to wounds from family?
The psalm moves from confident trust to urgent pleading. Where are you right now, and what would it look like to wait for the LORD in that place?
